topics.name: Medieval Kings - Who was the worst Medieval King?
facts: William the Conqueror was King of England 1066-1087 and was crowned on Christmas Day 1066, two months after defeating Harold at the Battle of Hastings.
William put Norman lords in charge of England, who built castles to defend themselves and their king, and he changed the language of government, business and the royal court to French.

In 1069 William carried out the Harrying of the North after northern rebels took Durham Castle, murdered the Norman earl Robert de Commines, and proclaimed Edgar the Aethling rightful King of England.
During the Harrying of the North, every village between York and Durham was burnt to the ground, crops were destroyed, fields were laced with salt, and an estimated 100,000 people starved to death.
In 1085 William ordered the Domesday Book, a survey detailing the possessions of every settlement in England so people could be taxed to pay for his armies and castles.
King John was King of England 1199-1216 and became king after his popular brother Richard I died fighting in France.

John captured his nephew Arthur, who also had a claim to the throne, and imprisoned him in a castle in France; Arthur was never seen again and was rumoured to have been tied to a stone and drowned in the River Seine.
John took 22 knights who supported Arthur, locked them in a dungeon in Corfe Castle and left them to starve.
In 1209 the Pope excommunicated John, meaning no English church could hold services, marry couples, baptise children or bury the dead, lasting five years.
John was nicknamed 'Softsword' or 'Lackland' as he lost nearly all English land in France, including Normandy.

In 1215 the barons forced John to sign the Magna Carta, which included not raising tax without the barons' permission, not imprisoning people without a fair trial (Habeas Corpus), and not controlling the English church.
John later declared the Magna Carta invalid, leading to civil war that ended only when he died in 1216.
Edward I was King 1272-1307, was raised on the battlefield, had 16 children, and was known for both charisma and cruelty.

In 1282 Edward I defeated Welsh prince Llywelyn ap Gruffyd, whose head was kept on a pike at the Tower of London for 15 years; Llywelyn's brother Dafydd was the first to be 'hanged, drawn and quartered'.
In 1296 Edward I conquered Scotland in just 21 days, earning the nickname 'Hammer of the Scots', stripped King John Balliol of his crown, and took the Stone of Destiny to London.

circle_prompts.question: Was William the Conqueror the worst Medieval King of England?

model_answer.words_from_question: One of the worst Medieval kings of England was William the Conqueror.
model_answer.evidence: He carried out the Harrying of the North in 1069 when the north rebelled against him. He marched his army north and burnt to the ground every village between York and Durham. Farm animals were slaughtered, crops were destroyed, and fields were laced with salt so that no more food could be grown, and around 100,000 people starved to death.
model_answer.explain_with_more_evidence: William also ordered the Domesday Book in 1085, which recorded the possessions of every settlement in England so he could tax the people to pay for his armies and castles, placing a heavy burden on his English subjects who resented a foreign king passing judgement on them.
model_answer.link: Therefore, William the Conqueror was one of the worst Medieval kings because he used brutal violence and harsh taxation to control England.

model_answer.link: Therefore, King John was one of the worst Medieval kings because he was cruel to his rivals and damaged England's relationship with both the Church and France.

topics.name: The Islamic Golden Age
facts: While most people in medieval Europe could not read or write and were exceptionally poor, the Islamic Empire was in a 'Golden Age'.
The caliphate was far reaching, and the common Arabic language allowed ideas and goods to spread easily.
The Prophet Muhammad said 'For every disease Allah has a cure', so Muslim doctors sought new treatments and herbs to heal people.
Ibn Sina (also known as Avicenna) wrote the 'Canon of Medicine', listing the properties of 760 different cures.
The 'Canon of Medicine' became the standard medical textbook used to teach doctors in Europe until the 17th century.
Soap, mirrors and magnifying glasses all came to Europe via the Islamic world.
Modern numerals (1, 2, 3...) and algebra came from the Islamic world; 'algebra' comes from the Arabic word 'al-jabr', meaning a reunion of broken parts or bone setting.
The lute (a stringed instrument) and the board game chess also came to Europe from the Middle East.
Many texts from Ancient Greece and Rome were preserved by being translated into Arabic.
Baghdad was built in 752AD as the new capital of the Islamic Empire.
Around 1 million people lived in and around Baghdad, which was built as a circle 1km in diameter with a mosque at the centre.
Baghdad had running water, beautiful gardens and schools of law; by contrast, London was a small muddy town with around 10,000 inhabitants.
In 830AD the 'House of Wisdom' library was built in Baghdad.
Muslim scholars in the House of Wisdom kept alive the classical texts of Ancient Greece and Rome by translating them into Arabic.
The House of Wisdom had more books than anywhere in the world and was an unrivalled centre for mathematics, astronomy, chemistry and philosophy.

topics.name: The Medieval Christian Church in England
facts: Almost every person in medieval England was a Christian and believed in God, the Bible, heaven and hell.
The head of the Christian Church was the Pope, who was believed to be God's representative on earth.
The Pope was very powerful across Europe, and the clergy believed they only had to answer to the Pope, not their king.
The Church owned one third of the land in England.
Through its monasteries and abbeys, the Church provided education, hospitals, historical records and welfare for the poor.
Monasteries and abbeys were religious houses in which monks and nuns lived to escape the corruption of the outside world.
By 1300 there were 900 monasteries and abbeys in England.
Most medieval people could not read, so popular religion was vivid, dramatic and colourful, taught through stained glass windows and wall paintings.
'Doom Paintings' in churches showed grim images of sinners being eaten, burnt, boiled alive, placed in chains and poked with spikes by the devil and his demons.
A pilgrimage was a journey to a place of religious significance.
The most important pilgrimage location in England was the tomb of Thomas Becket in Canterbury.
Wealthier pilgrims travelled to locations abroad, such as Rome or Jerusalem.
Pilgrimages could be dangerous and take years; pilgrims travelled in big groups to avoid being attacked and packed large amounts of supplies.
Pilgrims undertook journeys for forgiveness of sins, to be cured of disease or disability, or to gain good fortune.
At pilgrimage sites, relics containing body parts of saints could be prayed to, as they were believed to have miraculous powers.
